name: Pedro Lopez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Pedro. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for any company, union or party, and nothing you say will be linked to your name. Can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure. I'm on day shift this month, so the bus leaves the Carrow Street stop at 5:10 and gets us to the copper pit by six. I'm a trainee on the haul trucks, the big 220-tonne ones, so most of my day is driving loads from the shovel up the ramp to the crusher. A trainer named Hector still rides with me two days a week and marks my sheet.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the size of it. You come over the top of the ramp at sunrise and the whole pit is lit up orange, and you're part of that. What wears me out is twelve hours in a seat with the radio going and the dust, and knowing I'm still on the lowest pay band. My partner Lina is a care worker, so between us we cover the rent and not much else.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How much of your job is thinking work, like planning or paperwork, and how much is hands-on?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Almost all hands-on, or hands-and-eyes really. The dispatch system tells me where to go, so the planning is already done by a computer in the control room. My bit of paperwork is a pre-start checklist on a tablet, five minutes. Everyone at the mine knows the company is testing driverless trucks at its other pit up north, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay. Mostly hype. I can picture that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I say on the bus already: the bosses talk about tech, but the trucks still need us. I'd probably post something in the union group chat like, see, all that noise and we're still here. I'd keep it light.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, AI was never the thing coming for my job. The driverless trucks are, and those were being tested before anyone said AI on the news. So even if AI is hype, the company can still swap me for an autonomous truck. That worry doesn't go away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my hours and try to get signed off on the trucks by March so I move up a pay band. I'd also keep paying my union fees, which some guys skip. And I'd try to put fifty a week aside, though last time I tried that the car needed tyres.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly normal, a bit tight in the chest. Rent went up in August and we've got about two weeks of money in the account. That's the real pressure, not robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the driverless trucks are the real worry. What would that look like for you if they came to your pit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They'd start with the night shift, I think, because that's where the safety numbers are worst. Trainees like me get the night shifts. So I'd be first out, unless the union got a deal for us to retrain into the control room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If money got tight this year, what gets cut first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Takeaway on Fridays, that's the first thing, and Lina would hate it. Then the gym. We wouldn't miss rent, I'd ask my uncle for a loan before that, but I'd hate doing it.

say: I'd tell the bus crew the bosses **talk about tech**, but the trucks still need drivers.
I'd post in the **union group chat** that all that noise left us still working.
think: The real threat was never AI; it's the **driverless trucks** the company already tests up north.
With two weeks of money and **rent going up**, I'm tight even if nothing changes.
do: Get **signed off** on the 220-tonne trucks by March to move up a pay band.
Keep paying **union fees** and try to put fifty a week aside.
feel: Mostly normal, with a **tight chest** about rent and savings.
S0.quote: Even if AI is hype, the company can still swap me for an autonomous truck.
fieldNote: Pedro separates **AI hype** from autonomous trucks; he sees the trucks as a threat that exists either way.
His daily stress is **money**: a recent rent rise and about two weeks of savings.
Leans on the **union** as his main protection and expects night-shift trainees to go first.

steps.text: Finish truck sign-off with trainer Hector by March for the next pay band
Set aside fifty a week toward a one-month cushion
Keep paying union fees and go to the next branch meeting

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the next one. It's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right. So more real this time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's going to hit the office people first, the planners and the purchasing team. At the mine I'd tell the guys we need to get the union talking about the robots now, while it's slow. Online I'd share stuff about protecting workers, like I always do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think my job is safe for a few years and then it isn't. The planning side of the mine gets AI first, and that makes running driverless trucks easier and cheaper. So the slow robot part is the part that gets me. I'm 27, and I'd like a job I can still have at 40.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First, I'd ask the training coordinator about the control room course, the one where you watch the autonomous fleet on screens. I'd use the AI app on my phone to help me write that request, because my writing isn't great. And I'd push at the union meeting for a retraining deal written into the next agreement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but not stuck. There's time in this one, and I'd actually use it. It's the kind of change where if you move early you keep your seat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd use an AI app to write the request. Do you use those much?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now and then. I used one to write a complaint to the landlord about the mould, and it came out much better than mine. I don't trust it for facts, but for putting my words in order it's good.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The older drivers, honestly. Guys like Raul have twenty years on the trucks and they don't want to look at a screen all day. I'm young enough to switch. Raul has two kids in high school and a mortgage.

say: I'd say AI hits the **office jobs** first, like planners and purchasing.
I'd tell the crew the **union** should talk about robots now, while change is slow.
think: My trucking job is **safe for now**, then the cheaper planning makes driverless trucks easier.
At 27 I want work I can **still have at 40**, so I need to move early.
do: Ask the training coordinator about the **control room course** for the autonomous fleet.
Push for a **retraining deal** in the next union agreement.
feel: **Worried but not stuck**, because there's time to move early and keep a seat.
S1.quote: I'm 27, and I'd like a job I can still have at 40.
fieldNote: Pedro sees the link: AI planning makes **driverless trucks** cheaper to run, so his hands-on job feels it indirectly.
He uses **AI tools** to write, not to learn facts, and plans to use them for his course request.
He worries more for older drivers like Raul than for himself, showing **solidarity** rather than panic.

steps.text: Apply for the control room course for the autonomous truck fleet
Use a phone AI app to draft the course request letter
Push for a retraining clause at the next union branch meeting

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now a bigger one. It's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Wow. That's basically tomorrow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Publicly I'd be angry. I'd say this is the bosses and the tech companies deciding our lives without asking anyone. I'd be at every union meeting and I'd share every petition about a jobs guarantee or a robot tax.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, the AI part in 2028 doesn't touch my seat much, because I'm driving, not planning. But it means the control room job I wanted gets done by AI too. Then in 2031 the robots come and my truck drives itself. So I've got about five years, and the retraining door I was counting on closes first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now, I'd get my heavy-vehicle licence for public roads, because trucking outside the mine might last a bit longer. I'd keep every dollar I can. We'd move from our flat to a cheaper one near Lina's mum. And I'd be pushing the union hard for redundancy pay worth something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scary. Like being on the ramp and the brakes feel soft. You keep driving because you have to, but you're thinking about it the whole way down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Lina the night you heard?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her we're okay for now, because we are, for now. Then we'd sit down with the bank app and look at what we can drop. My partner Lina cares for old people, so her job might last longer than mine, which is funny because she earns less.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said trucking on public roads might last longer. Do you believe that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really, if I'm honest. Highway trucks will go driverless too, maybe a bit later than mines because of the rules. It's buying time, not a plan. But buying time is something.

say: I'd say the **bosses and tech firms** are deciding our lives without asking us.
I'd share every petition for a **jobs guarantee** or a robot tax.
think: The **control room job** I counted on goes to AI in 2028, before the trucks go.
Robots in 2031 give me about **five years** in the seat, no more.
do: Get a **heavy-vehicle licence** for public roads to buy some time.
Move to a **cheaper flat** near Lina's mum and save every dollar.
Push the union hard for **redundancy pay** worth something.
feel: **Scared**, like driving down the ramp when the brakes feel soft.
S2.quote: My partner Lina cares for old people, so her job might last longer than mine, which is funny because she earns less.
fieldNote: Pedro sees that his **escape route** into the control room is itself thinking work that AI takes first.
He admits the **public-road licence** is buying time, not a plan, which is an honest gap.
His partner's **care job** may become the household's steadier income, a reversal he notices.

steps.text: Get a heavy-vehicle licence for public-road trucking this year
Move to a cheaper flat near Lina's mum
Cancel the gym and Friday takeaway to save every spare dollar
Push the union for proper redundancy pay before 2031

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Same idea, a bit more time. It's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years for the AI. So robots around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same as before, but I'd add that five years is enough time for governments to do something if they want to. I'd be online saying, you've been warned, now act. At work I'd say we need a plan from the company, in writing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be about 35 when the robots take my truck. That's young enough to start again, but not with nothing. The difference from two years is I could actually finish a trade. I've always liked fixing the trucks more than I let on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now, I'd sign up for the heavy diesel fitter apprenticeship at the mine. It pays less at first, which hurts, but fitters will be needed to keep the robot trucks running, at least for a while. I'd cut spending to make up the drop and ask my uncle if we can stay with him for a few months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with a direction. Five years feels like a road with signs on it, not just a cliff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said fitters would be needed for a while. How long is a while?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't really know. Maybe until the robots can fix each other, and that's past 2034 in this picture, I think. It's still the best bet I can see from here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to the rent while you take a pay cut for the apprenticeship?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the hard bit. The first-year fitter rate is about four hundred less a month than I get now. Lina could take an extra shift, but she's already tired. Staying with my uncle for six months would cover it.

say: I'd say **five years** is enough warning for governments to act if they want to.
I'd ask the company for a **written plan** for workers.
think: I'd be about **35** when robots take my truck, young enough to start again.
With five years I could actually **finish a trade**, which two years didn't allow.
do: Sign up for the **diesel fitter apprenticeship** at the mine, despite lower first-year pay.
Ask my uncle if we can **stay with him** for six months to cover the drop.
feel: **Anxious but directed**, like a road with signs instead of a cliff.
S3.quote: Five years feels like a road with signs on it, not just a cliff.
fieldNote: The extra time turns Pedro from defending his seat to **choosing a trade**.
He admits a quiet liking for **fixing trucks** that he hadn't mentioned before.
The plan costs about **four hundred a month**, which his thin cushion can't absorb without family help.

steps.text: Sign up for the heavy diesel fitter apprenticeship at the mine
Stay with his uncle for six months to cover the pay drop
Ask the company for a written plan for affected drivers

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last one. It's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's a different feeling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, good, now there's no excuse. Ten years is long enough to build proper retraining and a safety net. I'd be pushing that line hard in the union and online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years plus three for the robots is 2039, and I'd be 40. That's exactly the age I said I wanted a job at. It's tight but it's fair warning. I'd still be worried, because companies don't wait for the deadline. They'll cut early if it's cheaper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the fitter apprenticeship over four years while Lina and I save a bit. Then I'd try to move toward electrical work, because that's in houses and towns, not only mines. Maybe we'd even think about a kid around 2030 if things look okay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but I could sleep. It's a long fuse. The danger is people think long means never.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said companies cut early. Have you seen that happen?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. When they brought in the new dispatch system, they cut two dispatcher jobs before it was even working properly. The guys who stayed had to cover the bugs. Companies cut early if it's cheaper, so I don't believe the date on a card.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned maybe a kid. Would this picture change that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It would push it back, I think. I'd want to be through the apprenticeship and in a job that isn't next in line. Lina wants kids sooner than me, so that would be a real conversation.

say: I'd say **ten years** leaves no excuse for missing retraining and a safety net.
I'd push for that line in the **union** and online.
think: Robots by 2039 means I'd be **40**, the age I wanted a job at.
Companies often **cut early** if it's cheaper, so the date on the card isn't safe.
do: Do the **fitter apprenticeship** over four years while we save.
Move toward **electrical work** in towns, not just mines, after the apprenticeship.
feel: **Uneasy** but able to sleep; it feels like a long fuse.
S4.quote: Companies cut early if it's cheaper, so I don't believe the date on a card.
fieldNote: Pedro remembers the **dispatcher cuts** that came before the new system worked, so he distrusts timelines.
Even with ten years, his **thin savings** and junior pay keep him anxious, not calm.
The scenario touches **family plans**: he'd delay children until he's in a safer trade.

steps.text: Complete the four-year diesel fitter apprenticeship
Move toward electrical work in towns after qualifying
Put off having a child until he's settled in a new trade

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, easily. The retraining door shuts before I can get through it. What would help is the company paying for apprenticeships while we're still on the trucks, at full pay, not the trainee rate. And some kind of wage support for people who have to start over.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who decides. That's what I'd want to know. A guy in a head office picks the date the trucks go driverless, and nobody at the pit gets a vote. If workers had a say in the timing, a lot of this would feel less like it's being done to us.

headlineQuote: A guy in a head office picks the date the trucks go driverless, and nobody at the pit gets a vote.
portrait: Pedro is a **trainee** haul truck driver at an open-pit copper mine, renting with his partner Lina, a care worker.
He has about **two weeks of savings** and already feels rent pressure, whatever AI does.
He sees **driverless trucks**, not AI chat tools, as the real threat to his seat.
With more warning he'd retrain as a **diesel fitter**; with two years he'd scramble for a road licence.
He trusts the **union** and wants workers to have a say in timing.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries him most, because the control room retraining route closes before he gets through.
whatWouldHelp: Company-paid **apprenticeships** at full pay while still driving, plus **wage support** for people starting over.
